lead: A decision problem is decidable when some Turing machine halts on every instance and answers yes or no correctly, and undecidable when no such machine can exist. Encoding machines and inputs as strings turns a problem into a language, and a mapping reduction carries undecidability from one language to another. This tells a programmer when to stop hunting for an exact algorithm: comparing two programs for identical behaviour, checking whether an arbitrary program ever reaches a given line, and building sound static analysers all run into these limits.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for recursive versus r.e. languages, and the decision procedures for DFA and CFG from Units 2 and 3.

blocks.text: A decision problem asks one yes-or-no question per instance. A Turing machine reads strings, not problems, so every instance is first written as a string. Fix an alphabet, encode every machine and every grammar as a string over it, and the set of yes-instances becomes a language L. Deciding the problem is exactly deciding L.

Write ⟨M⟩ for the code of a machine M: its states, tape symbols and transition table listed as one string. Write ⟨M,w⟩ for a machine together with an input word, with a marker between the two. Angle brackets always mean "the encoding of". A machine can read the description of another machine and simulate it, which is why these codes matter.

Three levels matter. A language is decidable (recursive) when a machine halts on every input and answers yes or no. It is partially solvable (recursively enumerable) when a machine halts and says yes on its strings but may loop forever on the rest. Some languages are not even r.e.: no machine lists their strings at all.
One fact links the levels: if L and its complement are both r.e., run the two semi-deciders in parallel and L is decidable — one of them must halt.
Decidable, using the machines built in earlier units:

items: DFA D: does D accept w, is L(D) empty, is L(D) finite, is L(D) = Σ*, is L(D1) = L(D2). Decide by running D, or by searching the product automaton for a reachable final state, a reachable cycle, or a reachable disagreeing state.
CFG G: does G derive w (CYK, Unit 3), is L(G) empty, is L(G) finite. These are reachability and parsing questions on the grammar itself.
A_TM = {⟨M,w⟩ : M accepts w}, the acceptance problem.
EQ_TM = {⟨M1,M2⟩ : L(M1) = L(M2)}, the equivalence problem.
P_TM = {⟨M⟩ : M, started on a blank tape, at some point writes the fixed non-blank tape symbol a}. This is undecidable: from ⟨M,w⟩ build M′ that simulates M on w and writes a only on acceptance.

blocks.text: Undecidable too, for context-free grammars, even though membership there is easy: whether L(G) = Σ*, whether two CFGs are equivalent, and whether G is ambiguous. Notice that for a DFA the corresponding questions (universality and equivalence of two machines) are decidable; the jump to a machine with unbounded memory is what destroys the algorithm.

A mapping reduction A ≤m B is a computable, total function f that turns every instance of A into an instance of B with the same answer. Some syllabi call this reducibility. The map needs no clever insight; it is usually a small program that copies a description and edits a few transitions.
A ≤m B  ⟺  there is a computable total f such that x ∈ A ⟺ f(x) ∈ B for every x
blocks.where: A and B are languages over one alphabet; f : Σ* → Σ* is computed by a Turing machine that halts on every input; ≤m is read "many-one reduces to".

blocks.text: (A ≤m B and B decidable) ⇒ A decidable;   (A ≤m B and A undecidable) ⇒ B undecidable
blocks.where: the second statement is the contrapositive of the first, and it is the one used in proofs.

items: Name the known undecidable language A (usually A_TM) and the target B.
Take a general instance of A; for A_TM that is a pair ⟨M,w⟩.
Describe the object that f builds, usually a new machine M′ whose code lies in B.
Prove both directions: the instance is in A exactly when the built object is in B.
Show f is computable and halts: it copies descriptions and adds a fixed piece of table, it never runs M.
Conclude that a decider for B would give a decider for A, so B is undecidable.

blocks.text: The built machine M′ is allowed to loop. Only f must halt. Confusing these two is the most common error in the exam.

figure.caption: The map f only writes the machine M′ down. M′ rejects every input except 101, and on 101 it accepts exactly when M accepts w, so M′ is in B exactly when ⟨M, w⟩ is in A_TM; a decider for B would therefore decide A_TM.

spec.aria: Top: ⟨M, w⟩ is mapped by f to ⟨M′⟩, and a decider for B on ⟨M′⟩ would decide A_TM. Below, M′ on input x: if x is not 101 it rejects, otherwise it simulates M on w and accepts if M accepts.

examples.question: Show that the language B = {⟨M⟩ : M accepts the string 101} is undecidable. Give the reduction explicitly and justify each part.
steps: Known undecidable partner: A_TM = {⟨M,w⟩ : M accepts w}. Take a general instance ⟨M,w⟩ of it.

Define f on ⟨M,w⟩. It builds a new machine M′ that works like this: on input x, if x is not the three-symbol word 101, reject at once; if x is 101, simulate M on w and accept exactly when M accepts w.
Why f halts: f only copies M's transition table and adds a fixed front part that compares x against 101, which costs at most 3 symbol comparisons. f never runs M or M′, so f halts on every input.
Forward direction: if ⟨M,w⟩ ∈ A_TM then M accepts w, so on input 101 the machine M′ accepts. Hence ⟨M′⟩ ∈ B.
Backward direction: if ⟨M′⟩ ∈ B then M′ accepts 101. By construction the only way M′ accepts any string is when it simulated M on w and M accepted, so ⟨M,w⟩ ∈ A_TM.
Therefore x ∈ A_TM ⟺ f(x) ∈ B, that is A_TM ≤m B.
Suppose B had a decider D. Then the machine "compute f, run D" would decide A_TM on every input and halt. A_TM is undecidable, so no such D exists.
examples.answer: B = {⟨M⟩ : M accepts 101} is undecidable, because A_TM ≤m B via the map ⟨M,w⟩ ↦ ⟨M′⟩, and a decider for B would decide A_TM.

traps: Writing "no algorithm is known" instead of "no algorithm can exist". Undecidability is a proved impossibility, not a gap in current knowledge.
Reversing the arrow. To prove B undecidable you reduce a known undecidable A to B, that is A ≤m B; proving B ≤m A proves nothing about B.
Thinking f must simulate M′. f only writes down the description of M′; M′ itself may loop forever, and that is allowed.
Mixing up undecidable with not r.e. A_TM is undecidable but r.e.; only its complement fails to be r.e.
Forgetting that f must be total and computable. A non-computable f would make the reduction worthless, and an f that loops gives no decider.

quiz.a: L is decidable (recursive) when some Turing machine halts on every input, accepts exactly the strings of L and rejects all others.
The encoding of a Turing machine M together with an input word w, written as one string with a separator, so that another machine can read both.

quiz.q: Why must the function f in a mapping reduction be computable and total?
quiz.a: Because the transformation itself has to be carried out by a machine. If f looped on any input the supposed decider could not finish, and the reduction would prove nothing about decidability.

quiz.q: If A ≤m B and B is undecidable, what follows about A?
quiz.a: Nothing. Undecidability travels from A to B along the arrow, not backwards; A could be decidable in that situation.

quiz.q: Show that C = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) is not empty} is undecidable, by reducing A_TM to it.
quiz.a: Map ⟨M,w⟩ to ⟨M′⟩ where M′ on any input x ignores x, simulates M on w, and accepts if M accepts w. Then L(M′) is non-empty exactly when M accepts w, since M′ either accepts every string or none. The building step is computable and halts because it only copies M's table. So A_TM ≤m C, and C is undecidable.

quiz.q: Which of these are decidable: (a) {⟨G⟩ : CFG G generates the empty string}, (b) {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅}?
quiz.a: (a) is decidable: simplify the grammar and test whether the start variable derives ε, or run CYK on ε. (b) is undecidable: E_TM is the standard emptiness problem for Turing machines.

quiz.q: A_TM is r.e. Why does that not make it decidable?
quiz.a: The semi-decider simulates M on w and halts with yes when M accepts, but it loops forever when M does not accept, so it never reports no. Deciding needs halting on both kinds of instance, and the complement of A_TM is not r.e., so no machine supplies the missing no answers.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, tools live with undecidability by giving up completeness: type checkers and abstract interpreters answer "yes", "no" or "don't know" and are built to stay on the safe side. Program termination and equivalence checkers used in industry work on restricted classes such as finite-state programs or linear loops. Search for decidable fragments, abstract interpretation and termination analysis if you want to see where this theory turns into engineering.
